A man hides witnesses in a grave to trap a debtor, who refuses; the scheme is an action beyond the ruling, but the rest is dialogue and ruling.
A claim, a counter-claim and contradicting witnesses, then a ruling; a court case with no further narrated change.
Rav Tovi asks Rav Yosef about his teruma wine and receives a ruling; question and answer only.
Rabba bar Rav Huna, in a dispute with the Exilarch's house, asserts his authority; speech only, but real conflict.
The emperor challenges Rabban Gamliel, who summons and strikes the servant to stage his answer; an encounter with conflict and action beyond speech.
A son steals flax sheaves, his father bars him from his property by vow and then modifies it when challenged; theft leading to a vow, with a ruling sought.
A prayer leader recites the service and Rava corrects the wording; speech and a correction with no further event or real conflict.

A man's aphorism and Shmuel's matching verse; speech only, no event or conflict.

Two estate cases: a bequest (speech) and a daughter's death, or a division of property, each followed only by rabbinic rulings and debate with no further narrated change.

Ulla's eyewitness account: a bird is brought, examined, the Nasi summons Ben Pazi and he leaves; real events, but weak causality and cited only as legal evidence.
A case (a man presumed to have no brothers) followed by legal debate between Rav Yosef and Abaye and Rava's ruling; no further narrated action or change.
Plague in Sura spares Rav's neighborhood; people attribute it to Rav, and a dream reveals it was a man who lent burial tools; events, a reversal and a revelation.
An incident in Nehardea is only mentioned, Rav Sheshet rules, and Rav Amram challenges with a sharp retort in reply; ordinary legal give-and-take.
A man's gift of a house turns out to hold 120 barrels and Mar Zutra rules; a case plus a ruling with no further action or change.
R. Zeira wishes to learn the halakha from R. Elazar, ascends to the Land, finds him and asks; a real journey, but the substance is teaching and dialogue.
R. Yohanan is told of elders in Babylonia and explains it; an exchange of speech with no event and no conflict.
Rabbi reports a deaf woman in his neighborhood who habitually examined stains, cited as evidence; a report of practice that leads nowhere.
A report of R. Yohanan's reading posture and the Gemara's explanation; no event.
R. Yohanan asks for his sandal, his attendant hands him the right one and he rebukes him; a small real incident, mainly speech, cited as evidence of his view.
Rav Mari brings a question about his cushions to Rava and gets a ruling; a setting plus question and answer is not a story.
In Rabbi's day a baraita is taught, everyone abandons Mishnah study and Rabbi then teaches the corrective; there is a collective event and a response, but it is mainly about teaching.
Bare reports, given as examples of a teacher: Rav Sehora explained a term and Shmuel rent his garment for a sage; nothing follows.
The Nasi dies and Rav Hisda gives an instruction; the outcome is only implied, so this is one event plus a directive.
Mareimar asks the students of Rav Yosef and Rav Sheshet who recited the Haggadah; question and answer cited as evidence.
A report of Hiyya bar Rav's and Rabba bar Rav Huna's habitual practice when dissolving vows; leads nowhere.
A creditor-debtor claim and a dispute between Rav Nahman and Rav Pappa; a legal case with rulings only.
A sage claims Job was a parable and R. Shmuel bar Nahmani rebuts with a verse; ordinary scholarly back-and-forth.
Rabban Gamliel's habitual weeping at the verse is an emotional event, but what follows is speech; the sages' reply lies in context. Mainly speech with one real event.
A woman comes before Rav Yirmeya and the rest is an exchange of claims about the receipt; coming before the rabbi is the only event and nothing changes.
Rabbi's report of what the students used to do for R. Shimon in Tekoa, cited as proof of discipleship; a habitual practice with nothing following.
Ben Azzai followed R. Akiva into the privy and learned from him, then a rebuke and reply; one real event with mainly speech and some conflict.
A man comes before Rabba with a question and Rabba rules; the coming before him is the only event, followed by a ruling.
An exchange between Antoninus and Rabbi in which the narrative content is a hypothetical parable; mainly speech, with the parable carrying the only events.
Reports of how Rav Kahana and R. Zeira broke bread on Shabbat, with a scholarly question and answer; practices cited as evidence, nothing follows.
R. Elazar b. R. Yosei's polemic against the Samaritans is speech only, but with real conflict against a sectarian opponent.
A fire in Drokart spares Rav Huna's neighborhood, people attribute it to him, and a dream reveals the true cause; several events with a change in understanding.
A woman tries to take dust from under R. Hanina's feet for sorcery and he responds with a verse; one real event and a spoken reply, no outcome narrated.
R. Zeira's death and a eulogizer's opening words, cited as evidence that Rakkath is Tiberias; one real event followed by speech.
R. Asi missed the study hall and asks R. Zeira what was said; the rest is ordinary scholarly back-and-forth without conflict or change.
A tanna recites a baraita before Rav Nahman, who challenges and attributes it; standard rabbinic dialogue, no event.
R. Eliezer entered the synagogue, found no quorum, freed his slave and completed the ten; multiple actions with a change, cited within the legal discussion.
Reports of Rav's and Mar b. Ravina's practice of not letting their sons treat them; habitual conduct cited as evidence, nothing follows.
A blind neighbor habitually judged and R. Yohanan said nothing; a practice cited as a difficulty, followed by legal discussion.
A Boethusian's disputation with R. Yehoshua HaGarsi ending in the sectarian's concession; all speech, but with sectarian conflict and implied change.
Rav Tahalifa tells Ravin what a dargash is; a lexical statement with no event.
R. Yehuda Nesia went out with a coral seal and drank gentile-heated water; R. Ami heard and was dismayed. Actions and an emotional reaction caused by them, then discussion.
A passing allusion to a giant snake in Shapur's time, cited as a counterexample; no narrated incident.
A man confined another's animal in the sun and it died (an act and a resulting change), followed only by a disputed ruling; minimal incident, then law.
Report of a halakhic tradition about expanding the altar; no narrated event involving people.
Rav Hisda's ruling challenged by Rav's grandsons and his answer is ordinary scholarly back-and-forth; the ruling is the only act.
A report of Ravina's father's habitual practice cited as evidence; nothing follows.
A Sadducee priest poured the libation on his feet and the people pelted him with etrogim: two actions with cause and change, told within the proof.
A public teaching plus Mareimar and Mar Zutra's habitual statement to gentile guests; a custom that leads nowhere.
Abaye finds Rav Yosef mourning and asks a question answered by a teaching; a setting plus question and answer, no conflict or change.
Rabbi Yehoshua married a priest's daughter and fell ill, then interpreted it; two events with implied causality but minimal development.
Rav sees Rav Kahana washing and sitting before him and rebukes him with a verse; mainly speech, but with events and a felt conflict (are you cursing me?).
A woman repeatedly brings witnesses who are refuted; on another occasion Reish Lakish glares angrily at Rabbi Elazar and rebukes him: multiple events, emotion and conflict.
Rabbi Zeira's death followed by a eulogizer's lament; one event then speech without development.
Rav Kahana briefly cites a personal incident (travelled home Friday, found no food) as evidence; one sketched event with a consequence.
A report that Reish Lakish eulogized a scholar with one line, cited as precedent; a single speech act, nothing follows.
A legal dispute and a retraction in light of an argument; speech only, ordinary scholarly debate.
An alleged incident (a bird hissed and a stone broke its head) cited as an objection in debate; alluded to, not narrated in full.
Ulla's habitual practice followed by Rava's textual objection; custom plus ordinary scholarly challenge.
An exegesis followed by the Sages casting their eyes on Rava b. Rabba; a passing allusion with no narrated event.
Rabbi and R. Yosei arrive at a field, one eats and one does not, the owner urges them and R. Yosei still refrains; events and interaction but little change.
Philosophers in Rome challenge the Sages about idolatry and receive an answer; speech only, but a polemical confrontation.
Mostly R. Zakkai's answer listing his practices, but it contains one event: his mother sold her kerchief to buy him kiddush wine.
Ulla sitting on a damaged platform is one act followed by a halakhic challenge and reply; ordinary scholarly back-and-forth with nothing changing afterward.
Rav Pappa's question, his teacher's silence and his own reasoning are speech acts within a legal discussion, with no conflict or event.
An exegetical narrative about Adam's reaction to God's decree; biblical characters, not post-biblical figures.
A setting (Rav Hamnuna searching for his oxen, meeting Rabba) frames only a question and answer, per the Shabbat 147a ruling.
A report of what Rav Ashi did with a collateral goblet, cited as evidence for a dilemma, with nothing following.
A description of Rav Yosef's agricultural practice and its result, cited to illustrate the baraita; no narrated incident.
A halakhic exchange between Ulla and Rav Yehuda and Rav Yehuda's later reflection; standard rabbinic dialogue without real conflict or event.
Foreigners came before Rava and he installed an interpreter, an act beyond a bare ruling, then legal discussion; segment 3 is only a legal exchange.
Ben Stada's smuggling of spells from Egypt is only alluded to as evidence in a debate, with genealogical discussion following.
Two incidents where judges seized slaves from orphans, and Rav Nahman's threatening order to return them; events plus a forceful ruling but no stated outcome.
One event (a bird falls into kutah), a ruling, and Rava's praise with legal reasoning; nothing else happens.
A visit framing a report of a past case and Rava's instruction to reverse it; ruling and discussion with the outcome not narrated.
Rabbi Yishmael's repeated refusals, the launderer striking him, and the resulting dissolution of the vow: multiple actions with causality and change.
A passerby's aphorism matched with a verse by Shmuel; speech only.
The Gemara's citation of the Mishnah incident of Rabban Gamliel's sons returning late, here only alluded to in one line.
A scholar retracts his view when shown a baraita; ordinary dialogue.
Rabbi Yirmeya visits, sees one practice, and rules it prohibited; a case and a ruling with no further change.
Rav Dimi brings a fat kid and then a lean one at Rabbi Yehuda's request before receiving a teaching; real actions but the passage is mainly about teaching.
Rava's exegetical narrative of Job's complaint and God's answer is about a biblical figure, cited inside a legal discussion.
Rabba finds Rav Huna eating porridge by hand and asks why; a setting plus a question and answer.
Rav Huna abolishes song and prices collapse; Rav Hisda belittles the ban and prices soar. Several actions with causal change.
A testimony and Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai's rejoinder: ordinary halakhic exchange with no event beyond speech.
Eyewitness incident of Rav Ashi examining a bird and splitting a sinew; real events but cited as evidence with little change.
Bare report that the rabbis passed the market and said nothing, cited as evidence of their view.
A man dies and Rav Nahman refuses to eulogize him with a quip; an event plus mainly speech with mild conflict.
An observation of the bird's behavior cited as grounds for a ruling; no narrative.
Rav visits and is served a fish prepared three ways; a report of what was done with nothing following.
Two first-person sea wonder sightings; real events narrated but little causality or change.
Contrasting habitual practices of Rav and Rav Amram Hasida; no one-time event.
Students question Rav's prediction and he answers; ordinary scholarly dialogue, no event.
A sale and dispute brought before Rav Yosef, followed by rulings and debate; coming before a rabbi is the only event.
Reish Lakish reports local vocabulary heard on a trip, used for exegesis; no narrative.
Rav Huna's contrary ruling angers Rav Yehuda and Rav Huna considers retracting; mainly speech but with emotional reaction and conflict.
A setting (the meat market) framing a halakhic question and answer; not enough for a story.
Within a Q&A, an incident of a ewe with a punctured windpipe sealed with a reed that lived is cited; minimal events and change, like the Chullin 57b hen.
Habitual practice of rabbis' wives cited as a challenge in legal discussion.
Rabbi Abbahu's own incident: he ate asafoetida, sat in water, and was saved; actions with causal change.
An anonymous incident cited as a difficulty: a single event (the fetus's spasms) with no change, inside legal give-and-take.
A man's instruction sent as a question to Rav Ashi, who rules; no other narrated action or change.
King Shapur challenges Rav Hama, who falls silent, and is criticized; speech with conflict.
Mar son of Ravina, thirsty, gets a miraculous spring and drinks: a protagonist, events and a change, but minimal and cited as evidence; like the splinted hen, a minimal story is borderline.
Lost meat brought before Rav Huna, question and answer, ruling; coming before the rabbi is the only event besides the loss and nothing changes afterwards.
Ameimar seats all the witnesses in deference to Rav Yeimar, an act that changes the courtroom, followed by a challenge and justification; more than a bare ruling but mainly discussion.
An incident: they forgot the scalpel and carried it over roofs on Shabbat; real events but little change or development, cited as precedent.
Meeting on the road, exchange of blessings, the rabbis fix their gaze on Rav Hanina and he dies: multiple events, conflict and a decisive change.
A case of an animal's anatomy, one rabbi inclines to rule, another objects; legal discussion with no narrated event.
Rav Yosef dozes at the lecture and sees in a dream the penitent received; a reported event with little development, embedded in a dictum about penitents.
Rav Ashi goes to cut his forest on the festival, is challenged, the ax slips nearly cutting his leg, and he stops until after the festival: actions, conflict and change.
Speech only: R. Yehoshua rules stringently, his students protest, he answers; there is some tension between teacher and students but no event beyond speaking.
A heretic challenges Rav Kahana and he retorts; pure dialogue but with real conflict (a sectarian challenge), so borderline under R-C2.
A halakhic question put to Rav and his answers; question and answer with no narrated event.
R. Yehuda cites a ruling of R. Tarfon as precedent, then legal discussion; the incident is a bare report of a ruling with nothing narrated.
R. Abba meets Rav's students and they exchange expositions of verses; a setting plus question and answer, ordinary scholarly dialogue.
An incident where flowers were removed and one fruit withered while the other survived; events with a change but no protagonist and cited purely as evidence, segment 3 is a halakhic conclusion.
A promissory note of orphans and Rav Hama's ruling; a case and a ruling, no narrated action.
Antoninus and Adrakan served Rabbi and Rav; at their deaths each sage laments; a habitual relationship, a death and a reaction with weak causality and little development.
An old man's custom of going out in a litter, a question to R. Yehoshua ben Levi and his ruling; a custom plus a ruling with nothing following.
The queen mother sends Rav Yosef a purse for a great mitzva; he deliberates and Abaye supplies the answer; one real event followed by discussion, with the outcome not narrated.
Abaye and Rav Yosef discuss leaving food on the stove, citing what Rav Yehuda, Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak and Rav Huna did as evidence; bare reports of practice inside legal give-and-take.
Cooked wine is brought, Ablet withdraws his hand, Shmuel tells him it is permitted; a small incident with an action and response but little change, ending in a halakhic statement.
A persecution decree is an event and R. Zeira responds by having the people take on a fast, but the rest is a question and a verse-based answer; mainly speech with little narrated change.
The Hasmoneans' candelabrum, iron then silver then gold as they grew richer, is a historical report cited as proof in a halakhic dispute; there are events and change but no developed narrative.
Rav Sheshet meets Rabba bar Shmuel and asks what he teaches, and Rabba bar Shmuel recites a baraita; a setting plus a question and answer is not a story.
A deathbed blessing exchange between R. Yehoshua ben Korha and Rabbi. It is mainly speech, but the setting is a real event and there is tension over the half-blessing.
Rav's order of washing, Shema, tefillin and prayer is a report of practice that the Gemara uses to work out the law; nothing follows from it except legal discussion.
R. Akiva asked an exegetical question of Rabban Gamliel and R. Yehoshua in the meat market. The setting only frames a question, so it is not a story.
A garden is fertilized with idolatrous dung, a query is sent and a ruling is given; one event plus a ruling, with nothing else changing.
An exegetical elaboration of Elisha, the youths and the bears; a biblical narrative, out of scope.
A habitual practice of Rav Hiyya son of Rav Avya, filling his hundred blessings with spices and fruit on Shabbat; a custom that leads nowhere.
That Ben Katin made twelve spigots is a bare report of a deed, cited as evidence in a legal argument.

A promissory note case is debated and ruled on by Rav Nahman. Rav Aha bar Yaakov suspects him of deflecting, then goes out, investigates and finds he was right: a little more than a ruling, but mainly legal discussion.
A Divine Voice answers Nebuchadnezzar's boast; an exegetical narrative about a biblical figure, out of scope.
The contrasting habitual market practices of Shmuel's father and of Shmuel, and an evaluation sent from Eretz Yisrael; customs with no event following.
Rav Yosef's statement about what he would have done, a festive day under either ruling, is speech about a hypothetical; no event is narrated.
A list of how three sages habitually protected their tzitzit when laundering; practices with nothing following.
Beloreya the convert asks Rabban Gamliel about a verse contradiction and R. Yosei the priest answers with a parable; a question and answer with no conflict or event.
A habitual wonder: birds flying over Yonatan ben Uzziel as he studied were burned. There are events and a consequence, but it is a one-line report with little development.
That Rav dissolved Rabba's vow standing, alone and at night is a bare report cited as evidence of Rav's view.
The table is removed before the child Abaye, he protests, and Rabba says his question has exempted them from Mah Nishtana: a one-time event with an action, a reaction and a resolution.

A man pays for dowry jewelry, the price then falls, and the parties come before Rav Pappa for a ruling, followed by legal discussion. Two events precede the ruling, but it is mainly a case and its law.
A man builds a mansion on the orphans' land, Rav Nahman orders him to appease them, he ignores it, and his mansion is confiscated: several actions, conflict and change.
Only an allusion to Shmuel's habitual practice, raised as a difficulty in the legal discussion; no narrated incident.
Levi demonstrates kidda before Rabbi and is injured: two events with causality and change, but minimal and immediately turned into discussion of the cause.
An exegetical narrative about God and the angels at the Red Sea, built on a biblical event.
Report of R. Yishmael ben Pabi's mother making a costly tunic which he wore and transferred to the public: several actions but little change, cited as illustration.
Rav Avya's illness and absence and Abaye's effort to placate Rav Yosef give real events and implied conflict, but the passage is mainly a halakhic dialogue.
One event (handing over a key) followed by a ruling, with no further narrated action or change.
Legal discussion; Rav Yehuda's demonstration with his hand is an explanatory gesture, not an event.
A quoted statement cited as evidence in a legal discussion; no narrated event.
Exegetical narrative about Balaam being blinded, a biblical figure.
A one-line report that 300 priests moved the vine, cited as an exaggeration; no change or continuation.
Two brief observations of rabbis praying or studying followed by a critical remark; ordinary rabbinic rebuke with no further event or change.
A report of Rav's commercial practice cited as evidence and then analysed; no one responds and nothing follows.
Rav Hisda's daughter immerses early in Rava's absence, catches cold and dies: a sequence of events with causality and change.
Rava's purchase is a setting for a halakhic challenge and answer; no further event or change.
Abaye throws a clod at the goats and Rabba rules he must return them: a real event followed by a ruling, with the outcome only implied.
Reish Lakish's argument against the Elders of the South is legal debate, speech only.
The Rabbis accuse Rava of taking interest and he rebuts them: mainly speech about his practice, but with a real accusation and conflict.
A setting (R. Zeira riding, R. Hiyya bar Avin walking) framing a question and answer and halakhic discussion; a setting plus Q&A is not a story.
Shabbtai pledges a cloak, the contract is lost, he denies it, witnesses testify, he claims payment, and R. Hiyya rules against him: several narrated actions resolved by a ruling.
R. Abbahu saw R. Abba of Akko's practice and changed his own; an observation leading to a change, but thin and cited as practice.
The Gemara's legal explanation of a story told elsewhere; no narrative here.
R. Akiva's travel report is cited as lexical evidence; nothing follows.
R. Shimon's remark leads to fasts and blackened teeth: some events and change, but tersely reported inside a legal discussion.
R. Yohanan's death and R. Ami's extended mourning are events, but the passage is then a halakhic comment on his practice.
A claim, a denial and the bringing of witnesses, followed by rulings; mostly litigation speech with little change narrated.
An animal brought before Rav Ashi, then legal discussion; coming before the rabbi is the only event.
A habitual practice of R. Ami and R. Asi cited as evidence; nothing follows.
The incident is merely named as the reason for a decree, not sketched at all.
Josiah reads a verse and hides the Ark: an exegetical narrative about a biblical king.
Rav's finding a scroll is cited only to introduce a teaching; nothing follows.
Ravina's dowry practice and an exchange with the groom's family; speech without real conflict or change.
R. Shimon b. Halafta sits on a rock, asks to be fanned, a wind blows and he quips: minimal events and change, little drama.
Reporting Rav's ruling to Shmuel and his sharp retort is ordinary scholarly back-and-forth.
A quoted instruction to a scribe used in legal argument; no event.
A partnership arrangement brought before Rava who permits it: one situation and a ruling, nothing changes.
Shmuel's message objecting to Rav's ruling is legal dispute in speech.
Sending an objection to a sage and the replies is standard scholarly dialogue.
Ulla's visit and the opened barrels are cited as a challenge within the legal give-and-take; nothing follows.
A setting plus a question shouted across a river and a halakhic answer; per the Shabbat 147a ruling not a story.
Objections and a report of Ameimar's opinion; pure legal discussion with no event.
One real act (Avin drags a bench) followed by R. Yitzhak's rebuke, which is speech with some conflict; little change narrated.
Rav Safra's face lights up and Rava responds; embedded is the cobblers' habitual conduct that leads to a change (the prostitutes swearing by them).
An army opened barrels and a case before R. Elazar was ruled permitted; one event then a ruling and discussion, nothing else changes.
Rava compares perforations and fails, his son rubs them and succeeds, explains, and Rava praises him: several actions with a change.
A convert comes before Rava and he rules; coming before the rabbi is the only event.
A damage situation followed by two rabbis' rulings; no further action or change narrated.
Josiah sequestering the Ark is a biblical episode retold exegetically.
An intention to teach and Rava's rebuke; speech and ordinary scholarly criticism, no event.
Rav Pappa transfers his debts, Rav Shmuel bar Aha travels and returns, and Rav Pappa goes out to Tavakh to meet him: several actions with an outcome.
Mainly offers and refusals in speech, but R. Yohanan's death intervenes and changes the outcome.
A bare report that Rav Ashi ruled a certain way in a case involving orphans.
Incidents only cited as precedents for rulings on stains inside a legal objection; no narrative.
Moses ascending on High and conversing with God is an exegetical narrative about a biblical figure.
Jeroboam's council and Ahijah's signing is a midrashic elaboration of a biblical episode; segment 4 is commentary.
Chaff harms people, they come before Ravina, he rules; nothing changes after the ruling.
A report of how Ulla bar Rav led the prayer and that Rava praised him, cited as evidence for the liturgy; no development.
A report that two rabbis travelling to Lod issued a ruling in Ono, cited for its halakhic content; nothing follows.
Minyamin's stated intention, cited as legal proof; speech only.
The Sages decide to appoint R. Abbahu and he defers to R. Abba of Akko; a real event with a speech-act response, little narrated change.
A question put to Rav and his ruling, then a follow-up question from his students; speech only, no event or conflict.
A prayer leader says 'emet' twice before Rabba and Rabba mocks him: one small event, mainly speech, with some conflict.
Rav Ashi and Rav Kahana's exchange about the absent Sages ends with Ashi learning it forty times, the same teaching-as-speech shape Jeff ruled borderline at Ketubot 50a:10.
Rav Nahman retracts his ruling in the morning and says he had been fasting: mostly scholarly dialogue, but with a narrated change of mind and its cause.
Rabbi Zeira's travels and encounters as he traces who said a halakha: real events (journeys, findings), but mostly about transmitting a teaching and with little change.
The dream is cited only to endorse an interpretation; the rest is ordinary scholarly objection and reply.
A tanna recites a baraita and Rabbi Yohanan rejects it sharply; that is ordinary rabbinic rebuke, not a story.
One act (dividing the peppers), then he comes before Rav Ashi and receives a ruling; nothing else happens, so under the 2026-10-25 limit it is not even borderline.
Rav Yosef's habitual Shavuot custom and saying; a custom that leads to nothing further.
A deathbed bequest is raised as a case, and Rav Nahman's visit only frames a legal question-and-answer; the visit is not a second event.
Teachings and students' questions with their answers; no event.
Shmuel steps off the road and Rav Yehuda's question gets a halakhic answer; a setting plus question and answer, cited as a precedent, with no change.
A habitual practice (praying in the Nehardea synagogue) is cited as evidence inside the legal discussion; it is a bare report.
Rav Shmuel bar Bisna goes from rabbi to rabbi and complains they all give the same answer: movement and some conflict, but mainly speech.
A dilemma resolved by an elder quoting a tradition; speech only.
A challenge answered with an insult; ordinary scholarly back-and-forth.
Tanhum arrives at Hatar, teaches, is challenged for ruling near his teacher, and excuses himself: an arrival and some conflict, but mainly speech.
A case before Rava, Rav Ilish's mistaken view, a rebuke, his embarrassment (which counts as an event) and the consoling verse: some change, but mainly speech around a ruling.
Rav Yosef weeps over a teaching and Abaye consoles him: an emotional reaction counts as an event, but it is mainly speech.
Rava gives his servant instructions about the time to light the Shabbat lamp; speech only, no event or conflict.
A deed signed by robbers comes before Rav Pappa bar Shmuel and Rava rules; no narrated action or change besides the ruling.
Rav Dimi's practice plus a briefly mentioned incident where the barrel burst; an event with minimal development, cited to support a rule.
Students ask and R. Shimon b. Yohai answers with a parable; teaching speech, no event.
Marta bat Baitos bribed Yannai to appoint Yehoshua ben Gamla: a real event with a consequence, but only reported in one line as evidence.
Rabbi rules, R. Yishmael cites his father, Rabbi defers; mainly speech with an implied change of ruling.
Hezekiah's father tried to burn him and his mother protected him: a biblical figure episode.
Baitos ben Zonin's exchange with the Sages over shaped matza is ordinary halakhic dialogue, no event.
Students request prayer and the rabbi replies; speech only without conflict or event.
A man's land purchase and request at division followed by Rabba's ruling; a case and ruling with no further narrated change.
A heretic's exegetical challenge and Rava's answer; ordinary scholarly exchange.
A report of Rav Yehuda's habitual practice cited as evidence of his view; nothing follows.
A man's proverb and Shmuel's matching verse; speech only.
A document with an odd date and R. Hanina's ruling; no narrated incident.
Eyewitness account: the prayer leader recites, the congregation tries to silence him, Mareimar intervenes and they stop; actions, conflict and change.
Avuh bar Ihi buys a loft, a creditor seizes it, he goes to Shmuel and challenges him; an incident with change and a ruling, the cow-case shape.
An actual incident: a man rents a donkey, the renter disobeys, the donkey dies, he claims no water; then Rava and Abaye rule on it.
Rabba bar Hana erred in a case and came before R. Hiyya, who ruled; one event then a ruling, nothing changes after.
Rav Yosef says he did not hear a tradition; a single statement.
A report that colleagues in the South agreed on two of three rulings; speech, cited as halakhic evidence.
Historical account of bathhouse attendants and bathers evading successive decrees and the Sages responding; multiple actions and change but generic actors and legislative framing.
Rav Sheshet hears a pestle and infers it is not from his house: one real event and speech, then Gemara discussion; little change.
A transmitted report that Rabbi permitted something, followed by ordinary scholarly challenge and answer; no narrated event.
A dying man writes a divorce and sighs, his wife promises to remarry him; real events and emotion but mainly speech, then a ruling with no further change.
Rabbi Hiyya's sons go to the villages, forget their learning and are distressed, then debate whether their father knows; events with change (the dialogue continues past the passage).
R. Yosei's lecture leads to 300 break-ins, people harass him, and at his death the gutters run with blood; multiple events and change.
Hananiah ben Azzur's false prophecy is a biblical episode retold; segment 3 is legal discussion.
A local custom reported to Rav Yosef and his ruling, then halakhic debate; coming before a rabbi is the only event and nothing changes.
A dialogue urging reprimand; speech only, no event and no real conflict.
Rav Natan loses and finds wool and asks Rav Hisda, who rules; a real event (loss) then a ruling with little else narrated.
Aivu's habit of eating gentile bread leads Rava to order him shunned; a habit with a consequence, but the consequence is a ruling.
A precedent of two rabbis' coin exchange cited only as a legal rule; no narrative.
A man kicks another's safe into the river and the owner claims its contents; real events, then an unresolved legal discussion with no outcome.
A tanna recites a baraita and Rav Nahman puns on his name; speech only, no conflict.
A sale statement and Rav Ashi's ruling on its meaning; no narrated event beyond speech.
R. Hama eats figs, his attendant refuses, and he tells him to eat citing a ruling; events but mainly a vehicle for a ruling, little change.
Rava's instruction to his attendant cited as evidence of his view, then legal discussion.
Ben Bukhri's testimony and Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai's rebuttal: scholarly disagreement, speech only.
Mainly dialogue, with R. Zeira's harm (carrying myrtle to the king's palace) only alluded to.
Reports of Rav Kahana's and Ravina's practices with gentiles cited as evidence for a ruling; nothing follows.
Asked a question, R. Hiyya bar Abba is silent and next day publicly teaches; mainly speech/teaching with slight development.

Rav Oshaya travels to Eretz Yisrael and twice meets Rabbi Ami. Their exchange is mainly speech, but it contains real conflict (the oaths 'By God!'), so it is borderline; segments 4, 6 and 7 are legal discussion.
An apostate's challenge and Rabbi Abbahu's answer. This is a question and answer with no narrated event.
Rava bar Shmuel visits the Exilarch and breaks bread against his own ruling, then is questioned and explains. There is one real event, followed by speech and a ruling.
A secondhand report that the Sages dissolved a vow and told the man to pray, cited for a legal point. It is a case and a ruling with no further narrated change.
An injury case comes before Rava and he rules, followed by ordinary legal challenge. Coming before the rabbi and his ruling is the only development.
A setting (walking, being brought into Rav Safra's house) that frames a halakhic question and answer, then a report of it. Like Shabbat 147a, this is not enough for a story.
Rav Asi's face lights up with joy (an emotional event), and Rabbi Yohanan deflates his answer. It is mainly a fragment of dialogue with a small reaction.
Rabbi falls ill and forgets his learning. Rabbi Hiyya restores it, including by learning from a launderer, and Rabbi then honours the launderer: several actions with clear change.
A man is attacked by a lion and miraculously rescued, then comes to Rava, who instructs him. There are narrated events and a change beyond the ruling, like the cow case.
An exegetical narrative about Abraham and God built on the biblical verses. This is a biblical figure, not a rabbi.
Abaye reports what he saw at Rabba's house as evidence for a halakha. It is a bare report of practice with nothing following.
Rabbi Yirmeya is sent to ask Rabbi Avin and does so. This is scholarly back-and-forth made of quasi-speech acts, without conflict beyond normal debate.
Rav remarks to Rabbi Hiyya and is told how Rabbi recited Shema: a description of practice in dialogue, with no event.
A man comes before Rav Huna, answers one question, and the vow is dissolved. This is a case before a rabbi and a ruling, cited as legal precedent.
First-person reports of carrying Rav Huna and Shmuel in a chair, cited as evidence of practice. Bare reports with no continuation.
Shmuel recalls the day the king's army came, the Sages could not pray, and he prayed alone. There are real events, but the incident is a brief report cited as evidence, with little development.
Shmuel's father repeatedly sends notched knives to ask a question and receives an answer. Sending a question is quasi-speech, and nothing else happens.
Abaye's mother's custom of raising a lamb, followed by Gemara discussion. It is a habitual practice that leads nowhere.
Mustard is prepared and refused, and Ze'eira's wife challenges the student. There are events and a confrontation, but they are brief reports cited as evidence, with weak causality and little change.
A death befalls Rabba bar bar Hana and he is advised twice about lecturing while in mourning. There is one real event; the rest is speech and rulings.
Fasts are decreed and rain falls (real events), but what follows is a halakhic correction and Shmuel HaKatan's parable; mainly speech with little change.
A question and answer, plus a bare report that ben Elasa spent money on a haircut; nothing follows.
A halakhic query sent and answered twice; quasi-speech acts with no event or conflict.
A report of Shmuel's transaction cited as evidence for his ruling; no one responds and nothing follows.
Tenant farmers stole and Rav Zevid disqualified them as witnesses: real events plus a ruling that is itself an act, but minimal narrative development.
A certain man coerced by gentiles shows and carries Rav Mari's wine, then Rav Ashi rules and defends his ruling: an incident with several actions resolved by a ruling, R-C0's cow shape.
R. Elazar's instruction to his attendant is cited as his practice; no event follows.
An exegetical narrative about Abraham, Eliezer and God at the tent; biblical characters.
A bare report of how Rav acquired the garden, cited as proof of his ruling.
R. Yohanan rebukes a recitation of a baraita; ordinary scholarly speech, not conflict in R-C2's sense.
Someone disparages the late Mar Shmuel and a reed falls and fractures his skull: two events with implied causality and change.
The people of Nineveh send a halakhic question and Rabbi answers; question and answer only.
An elder explains a teaching to R. Ami; pure speech.
A visit that only frames a halakhic question about a mezuza; setting plus question is not a story.
Incidents alluded to only as precedents for rulings; one event then a ruling, nothing narrated.
R. Yehoshua's instruction to his sons is cited as practice and then analysed; no event.
R. Yehoshua sends word that R. Yishmael erred and states his view; ordinary halakhic dispute.
Avimi's arrival only introduces a baraita; legal discussion.
Rav Pappa bar Shmuel's instruction to his attendant and Rava's halakhic correction; setting plus ruling, no further event.
Two students each prevent R. Yitzhak Nappaha from teaching, and he answers with a parable; conflict, but mainly speech.
Rabba bar Rav Huna visits the Exilarch and recites the blessing with two endings; Rav Hisda derides it. One real act followed by a scholarly challenge, mainly speech.
A suggestion in debate and the Sages laughing at him; speech with conflict (being mocked), no event beyond speaking.
The grandson comes before R. Yannai, who asks a question and dissolves the vow; coming before a rabbi and his ruling is the only event.
Reports of what Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Yannai did, met with interpretive remarks; bare reports and ordinary dialogue, nothing follows.
Abaye recounts reclining on each other's knees at Rabba's and Rav Yosef telling them they need not recline; real events but mainly a ruling cited as proof, weak change.
A habitual practice of Rav (washing, blessing, teaching) cited as evidence; a custom that leads nowhere.
A seller announces a price, a buyer deliberately overpays to sue, and the case comes before Rava who rules; multiple narrated actions followed by a ruling, the cow-case shape.
Rabbi Yishmael reports what an angel told him: a list of teachings framed as speech, no event.
The rabbis enter Yavne and each speaks in honor of the hosts; a setting framing a series of homilies, mainly teaching (speech), with the intervening segments being exegetical commentary.
Rav Pappa permits Rav Avya to teach and a teaching follows; a teaching, not an event.
A famine and plague in R. Shmuel bar Nahmani's days and a debate on what to pray for; a real situation but the passage is all deliberation with no narrated outcome.
A man promises land at a price, then sells it to another for more, and the rabbis rule; two narrated actions and a change followed by a ruling.
Rav Geviha teaches, Ameimar challenges, Rav Ashi answers; ordinary scholarly back-and-forth, not conflict.
Rabba bar Rav Huna makes a tambourine for his son, Rav Huna comes and breaks it and instructs him; multiple actions and a change.
A habitual remedy the rabbi would apply to drunk students; a custom cited as evidence with no one-time event.
A single wondrous event (wheat raining on Adi the Arab) cited as proof; a real event but no response or development.
Rabbi Zeira's instruction to his servant, cited for its halakhic inference; speech only.
A setting (finding Rav Yehuda cheerful) followed by questions and answers; per Shabbat 147a a setting plus Q&A is not a story.
Shmuel threatens myrtle sellers who overcharge; speech with conflict and implied change, but no narrated outcome.
A dog eats the Sages' shoes, they excommunicate the unknown culprit, and the dog's tail burns; multiple actions with causal change.
A sale and a dispute over what it included come before Rav Nahman, who rules, and Rava challenges. There is a transaction plus a ruling, but little change beyond the ruling.
Rabbi Yohanan recalls an exegetical teaching that was later confirmed. This is teaching and speech, with no event.
A report of Rabbi Yohanan's habitual practice before answering questions, cited for a halakhic point. Nothing follows from it.
Levi bar Buti stammers while reading and Rav Huna states a halakha. This is one event followed by a ruling, with no further change.
An anonymous man's aphorism about love, with verses that parallel it. Speech only, no event.
An exegetical exchange between the prophet Ezekiel and ten people, with God's reply. It concerns biblical figures and is mostly dialogue.
Rav Kahana passes a locust near his mouth and Rav tells him to put it down. A single act and an instruction, cited inside a legal argument, with no change.
Rabbi cried out against people kneading shatit; no one listened, and he could not prohibit it. There is conflict and some events, but it is mostly reported speech with little development.
Rav Hisda's advice and his personal practice of not eating vegetables. A habitual report that leads nowhere.

Three priests describe their portions; one uses impure imagery, and an investigation finds a flaw in his lineage. The speech leads to an investigation and a discovery, so there are events and a change.
Rav Sheshet's habitual practice of studying during the Torah reading, with his justification. A bare report of a practice.
A halakhic dilemma, a disagreement, and a question put to Rava, who answers. Ordinary scholarly question and answer.
Shmuel's father's habitual practice for his daughters' immersion, cited and explained for its halakhic basis. Nothing follows from it.
An incident (a fetus moving after its mother's death) is only alluded to as evidence in a legal discussion and then explained away.
A man who took a slaughtering knife as collateral comes before Abaye and receives a ruling, and Rava disagrees. One event, then a ruling.
A case of conflicting testimony came before Rabbi Ami, who ruled. A case before a rabbi with his ruling, and nothing else narrated.
Rav Pappa reports that Rabba tested his students on a legal question and the exchange that followed. Scholarly dialogue only.
An exegetical teaching that God showed Moses three things he found difficult. It concerns a biblical figure, and there is minimal narrative.
Rabbi Akiva's reports of words he heard on his travels, used for lexical exegesis. No event develops.
Shmuel has ten men gathered so that he can publicize a halakha. The act only frames the statement of a ruling.
Rabbi Elazar's question is followed by an act: he goes out, searches and finds the source. That is one real event, but the passage is mainly about learning, which counts as speech.
Brief eyewitness reports ("I once went to the Galilee and saw...") cited as evidence. One-line eyewitness accounts are an open case, so this goes to borderline rather than not.
A real incident is cited in very compressed form: the daughters went ahead of the sons and were found zealous. It has an event and an outcome but almost no development.
Ordinary scholarly exchange: a challenge and Ulla's reverent reply, with no event.
A halakhic debate between R. Eliezer and R. Yehoshua that ends with Eliezer falling silent. This is standard rabbinic dialogue with no event beyond speech.
An eyewitness report of one anomalous case in the rabbi's neighbourhood, cited as evidence. There is minimal change and no response, so it sits between not and borderline.
An exegetical statement that Gabriel showed Moses the Menorah: a single act about biblical figures, with no development.

Bar Liva'ei sees Mar Ukva applying salve and objects; R. Yannai asks for salves and Mar Ukva sends them with advice. There are some real actions, but the passage is mostly speech and halakhic comment.
A son corrects his father's version of a teaching and Shmuel rebukes him. This is ordinary scholarly back-and-forth and rebuke, all speech.
An exegetical narrative of Elisha going to bring Gehazi to repentance, which Gehazi refuses. The characters are biblical.
R. Yoshiya reports rulings he received and that his colleagues accepted two of them. This is transmission and disagreement of teachings with no conflict beyond normal discourse.
R. Yirmeya's jab at the Babylonians and Rava's response are standard rabbinic dialogue around a halakhic argument, with no event.

R. Yehuda Nesia twice sends a firstborn animal for examination, and each time another rabbi steps in with the halakhic rule. There are real actions with some conflict, but the outcome is only implied and the passage is mostly rulings.
Exegesis of Moses' rebuke of Israel: speech by biblical figures, built from verses, with no narrated event.

Ulla rides with R. Abba and Rabba bar bar Hana. When a misattribution comes up he turns and glares at Rabba bar bar Hana, who explains himself, and the matter is resolved. There are actions, conflict and resolution.
Ravin reports a teaching and R. Yirmeya derides the Babylonians and cites a counter-tradition. This is ordinary scholarly dialogue.
A setting (sitting before Rabbana Nehemya, who wears silk) frames a terminology question and answer. A setting plus Q&A is not a story.
R. Yohanan meets a man picking unripe figs, asks him why, and the answer gives him a new understanding of a verse. There is an encounter, a dialogue and a change.
The Sages prayed and the sound of the departing soul was abolished. There is an act and a change, but it is told in a single line with no protagonist or development.

An ox falls into a channel, its owner slaughters it, Rav Nahman declares it tereifa, and he remarks on the owner's needless loss. This is an incident with actions followed by a ruling, the cow-case shape.
Wine placed with sharecroppers is one event, followed only by the Rabbis' and Rava's legal reasoning; nothing further happens.
A man sent silk home and Rabbi Ami ruled on its division; one event plus a ruling, no further change.
Rabbi Zeira's first-person report of eating in the sukka and rejoicing, cited as evidence; nothing follows from it.
Ravina arranges his son's match, agrees a date, then delays the wedding a week; multiple actions and a change that the following dialogue continues.
Rav Yosef falls ill, forgets his learning, and Abaye restores it to him; several events with causality and change.
A question and a dismissive answer; speech only, of the ordinary question-and-retort kind, with no event.
Mainly a halakhic dialogue, but with a narrated frame (Rava dozing, then waking and intervening).
An exchange of insults between two midwives: speech only, but with real conflict and an implied history of acts.
Fat fell into a pot and Rav Asi proposed a measure that the Rabbis challenged; one event then legal discussion.
Exegetical narrative about Joshua and the angel, a biblical episode elaborated by the Gemara.
Rav Adda bar Ahava's habitual practice of salting bone by bone, cited as practice; nothing follows.
Cases brought to Rabbi Yohanan (roasted kid, fish in a pot) each with only his ruling; one event then a ruling.
Rabbi Akiva's intercalating in prison is a single act cited as evidence and immediately discussed; no continuation.
Isi bar Hini's arrival and Rabbi Yohanan's corrections and rebuke over 'Abba the tall' are mainly speech, but with conflict and a narrated encounter.
Elijah and Rav Yehuda exchange questions and answers about the messianic date; speech without event or conflict.
Mareimar and Mar Zutra's practice of rebuilding synagogues, cited to illustrate the law; a report of practice with no continuation.
A halakhic objection and a report of a vote; legal discussion, no narrated event.
An encounter that only frames a scholarly question and answer with courteous exchange; ordinary rabbinic dialogue.
Rava's illness and the visit only set the scene for a legal discussion; a setting plus question and answer.
An eyewitness report of Rabbi Yohanan's practice, cited as evidence in a legal argument.
Reports of Rabba's practice that changed after he heard a teaching; there is a change but it is cited as evidence for a ruling with little narrative development.
Rahava brings orphans' money before Rav Yosef, who rules, is challenged by Abaye and reverses himself; mostly speech and ruling, but the ruling changes, which gives some dynamism.
A bare report of what Rabbi Tzadok did, quoted from the Mishnah as proof in a legal discussion.
An exegetical narrative about Israel in the wilderness and the prophets' enactment, built on a biblical episode.
A dialogue between Moses and Pharaoh's magicians: biblical characters, and speech only.
Rabbi's report that he read the Megilla as a minor is cited as proof and rejected in legal argument; nothing follows.
An incident only alluded to, consisting of a single ruling by Rabbi and cited as an objection; no other action or change is narrated.
Brief citations that Rava and Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak imposed fines, offered as precedents with no narrative.
An exegetical exchange between the biblical king Amon and his mother.
Ravina asks Rav Ashi a question and receives a ruling; coming before a rabbi is the only event.
A man comes before Rav Yeimar, who rules that his phylacteries are to be taken; it is a case followed by a ruling, with no further narrated change.
A deed is brought for adjudication, followed by Rabba's ruling and Abaye's objection; it is legal discussion with no further event.
Mar Zutra Hasida's habitual practice, cited to illustrate a ruling; the custom leads nowhere.
The Sages challenge Rav Sheshet, he becomes angry and retorts; it is mainly speech, but has conflict and an emotional reaction.
Rav Gaza's one-time anecdote, in which he prepared kutah and the sick of the West asked for it, has two minimal events, though it is cited as evidence within banter.
One event (Rav Huna's crop harvested), then his son's halakhic objection and his answer; ordinary legal discussion with nothing changing.
One day Mar Ukva, preoccupied, fails to notice Shmuel accompanying him; Shmuel speaks, Mar Ukva realizes he offended him and imposes admonition on himself, so there are actions, conflict and change.
A report of Shmuel's father's habitual practice for his daughters' immersion; nothing follows.
Rav Nahman's childhood memory of a court announcement, cited as evidence for Shmuel's ruling; no story develops.
Rabbi Zeira's habitual practice of urging the Sages not to desecrate Shabbat; a custom and speech that lead nowhere.
Rava's visit and remark about the breaded goose is cited as evidence within the legal give-and-take; a setting plus a statement with nothing following.
Abaye sees Rava gazing west and they exchange an interpretation of a baraita; ordinary scholarly dialogue without conflict or change.
A tanna recites a baraita and Rabbi Elazar questions its meaning; standard study-hall dialogue, no event beyond speech.
Rabbi reads Lamentations, the book falls from his hand in distress and he exclaims; real events and an emotional reaction but minimal development.
The visit to Rav Hisda's house where a duck is moved is cited as evidence of his ruling; a reported practice in the legal discussion, nothing follows.
Ben Dama asks Rabbi Yishmael a question and receives an answer by verse; a question and answer with no event.
Rav Kahana's frame (sitting, hearing, asking the students) only introduces a halakhic teaching; speech without conflict or change.
A polemical exchange between the Romans and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya; speech only but with adversarial conflict and a partial concession.
Rav Mari's eyewitness account: angels disguised as sailors turn sand into flour, people come to buy, he warns them off; multiple narrated events with a miraculous change.
Rabbi Eliezer b. R. Yosei recounts refuting the Samaritans; a polemical confrontation that is essentially speech, with conflict.
Rabbi Hanina attributes his son's death to cutting down a fig tree prematurely; two events and causality, but only alluded to as support for a law.
Rabbi Abbahu teaches and Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi turn their faces away in protest; a gesture of conflict, mainly a teaching scene.
Shmuel threatens the pot merchants who raised prices; speech with real conflict and an implied change, but no narrated outcome.
Rav Haviva states a difficulty and a sage rebukes him and explains; a rebuke within ordinary scholarly back-and-forth.
A man in the market calling out 'who wants ahvana' is a lexical anecdote cited to explain a word; a bare report with no development.
Rav Beivai twice plans to complete his Torah portions and is corrected each time; a change of intention, but essentially teaching and speech.
Rav Yosef turning his face away is a single gesture of disagreement, followed by the Gemara's explanation; ordinary scholarly disapproval.
Rav's finding a hidden scroll at Rabbi Hiyya's house is only the source citation for a halakhic statement, which is then debated.
A habitual scene: schoolchildren sent to Hanan HaNehba to ask for rain and his prayer; habit with a prayer but the outcome is only implied.
A report of Rabbi Hanina's ability at eighty and his explanation of it; description of a state, no event or development.

A man showed the Exilarch's wheat to thugs who seized it, the case came before Rav Nahman who held him liable, then a scene of questioning; like the cow case, the incident has its own actions before the ruling.
Mainly a question and retort, but R. Shimon throws a clod at the questioner: one real act with conflict, little development.
Ordinary halakhic debate between R. Yohanan and Reish Lakish and later discussion; silence and teaching are speech, no event.
A dictum from a notebook about those born on Sunday; no event.
Rava's permission is cited only as a precedent ruling; nothing else happens.
A passerby's proverb and Shmuel's verse; speech without conflict or event.
R. Yohanan's habitual practice and his explanation to the Sages; a custom that leads to no change, the rest is dialogue.
A report of Rav Hisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna's practice cited as evidence in a halakhic discussion.
Mishnah and Gemara glosses; R. Elazar b. Azarya's cow is a custom with no event, and the Rav Hisda quips are ordinary scholarly dialogue.
An eyewitness report of Ze'iri crossing a river, cited as evidence and disputed; a bare report.
The rabbis' practice of praying in the Nehardea synagogue is cited as evidence; no incident develops.
A habitual practice (studying Sefer Yetzira) that produces a wondrous result, a calf created and eaten; events but minimal development.
Ulla's visit only frames his identification of hyssop; setting plus statement, as in Shabbat 147a.
An animal slaughtered irregularly and a rabbi demonstrates its validity by taking meat, then Rabbi Zeira comments; an act-ruling with limited change.
A man's will statement and Rav Pappa's ruling; speech then ruling, nothing happens.
Levi comes before Rav Sheshet and receives a ruling; coming before a rabbi is the only event.
A gentile jumps up and plugs a leaking barrel, then Rav Pappa rules; real actions but followed only by a ruling and discussion.
Rav Hisda finds Rav Hananel writing Torah scrolls from memory and corrects him; one real event, mainly speech, then Gemara discussion.
Rav Huna's acts of artifice (garlic in the spout, sleeping on the ferry) are reported to Rav Ashi, who answers; events, but mainly a report and a ruling.
Rav Hisda meets Rabba bar Shmuel and asks a question that is answered; question and answer only.
The Sages suspect Rava, then Shapur's men imprison him, and he reads it as the fulfilment of the baraita. There are several actions and a change.
A public teaching is followed by Rabbi Ami's anger and rebuke. It is mainly speech, though the anger is a reaction and there is conflict.
Rabbi Ya'akov is ill and receives remedy instructions, followed by a list of cures. Nothing else is narrated and nothing changes.
Ravina's request to his mother only frames a halakhic challenge and answer. This is ordinary scholarly dialogue with no event that changes anything.
An eyewitness report of the rabbis eating fruit without washing or inviting him is cited to derive three laws. There are events but little change; it sits between a report and a story.
A document's ambiguity is sent to Abaye and he rules. Coming before a rabbi for a ruling is the only event.
A student's habitual restraint leads Rabbi Yannai to apply a verse to him in praise. The habit draws a response, but the response is only speech, so there is little change.
The setting (arriving early at the wedding) only frames teaching and a halakhic exchange with Rami bar Hama. This is a setting plus question and answer.
A bloodied duck in Rava's house prompts deliberation and his son's suggestion, used to derive the law. One event is followed by legal discussion, and no outcome is narrated.
Rabbi decides afflictions are precious and takes thirteen years of illness upon himself. This is an action with consequences, part of the larger narrative around it.
Shammai the Elder refuses to feed with one hand, and the Sages respond with a decree compelling him. A practice draws a response that changes his conduct.
Rava's disparaging gesture and rebuke of Rav Shimi is part of an ordinary halakhic challenge, which is standard Talmudic discourse.
Rav Hamnuna demands an answer and Rabbi Zeira gives it. This is a question and answer only.
It reports the habitual hiring practice of rabbis as halakhic precedent. Nothing follows.
A general historical statement about how Torah was studied before and after Rabban Gamliel's death. No incident is narrated.
A man plants wheat instead of sesame and earns more, and the rabbis then discuss the ruling. There are real events, but what follows is legal discussion with no further change.
Rabbi Hiyya insults Rabbi Shimon, who goes to his father, and the father supplies a retort. It is mainly speech, but there is real personal conflict and an action.
Eyewitness reports and lists of what various rabbis wore on Yom Kippur, cited as evidence for the law. These are bare reports of practice.
An exegetical narrative about Micah's idol, the angels and the men of Gibeah. These are biblical figures.
A disciple asks Rabbi Eliezer questions and receives answers, followed by Gemara analysis. This is question and answer only.
Agra comes before Rabbi Abba with a scroll question and receives a ruling; coming before a rabbi is the only event, nothing else changes.
A bare report that Rav Huna and Rav Adda declared produce ownerless, cited as evidence in the legal discussion; nothing follows.
A list of recollections of past conditions (prices, abundance, modesty), descriptive reports with no narrated incident or change.
A dead mouse found in Rav Ashi's storeroom and his instruction to remove it, cited as a legal proof; one event and an order, with the outcome only implied.
Disciples ask and Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua answers; a question and answer with no event and no conflict.
A habitual feat of strength by the son of Marta bat Baitos, met by the priests' refusal to let him; real actions and some conflict but habitual and with little development.
An incident in Mar Shmuel's house (gizzard would not peel, set in the sun, then peeled) with two events and a change, but minimal and cited as evidence in a legal discussion.
Rav Giddel's habit of sitting at the immersion gates, challenged by the Sages and answered; mainly speech around a habitual act, with some conflict.
A tanna recites a baraita before Rav Adda bar Ahava who corrects it; ordinary scholarly exchange, speech only.
Yohanan the High Priest's sending of emissaries and discovery is only alluded to as the reason for a law; real events, but sketched rather than narrated.
Shmuel reports asking seafarers about eshlag and their answer; a lexical identification via speech, no event.
Rabbi Yohanan overhears a maiden fall on her face and pray; a single eyewitness incident cited as a lesson, with little change, between report and story.
The Elders of Pumbedita ask Rav Yosef to teach them, he has them teach him first, and then refuses; an exchange with an action and a twist that changes the outcome.
Rabbi Yohanan's silence and the hypothetical analysis of what he could have answered; legal discussion, no story.
Transmission of a statement and Rav Sheshet's dismissive gesture; standard scholarly reaction, not an event.
Rabbi Akiva visits Ginzak, cannot answer three questions, and goes to the study hall to learn the answers; some movement and change but mainly questions and teaching.
Reports of the habitual examination practices of Rabba bar Avuh and Rabbi Hanina and a curse with explanation; customs that lead nowhere.
The Alexandrians' questions to Rabbi Yehoshua and his answers, followed by legal analysis; a question-and-answer frame, not a story.
Jugs of wine found among vines and Rava's ruling permitting them, followed by legal discussion; one event then a ruling.
Ronya buys adjoining land, Ravina considers removing him and Rav Safra tells him he cannot; one event followed by a legal ruling with nothing changing after.
A report of Rav Nehemya's examination practice, cited only to debate which ruling it attaches to; nothing follows from it.
A document is brought before Rav Huna's court and he rules; Rav Hisda's instruction to Rabba is speech. A case and a ruling, with no further narrated change in the passage.
The torn strap only frames a halakhic question and answer between Abaye and Rav Yosef; a setting plus Q&A is not a story.
A man strikes another and is ordered by R. Yehuda Nesia to pay; an incident plus a ruling, cited as legal proof, with the outcome only implied by the order.
Rav Huna eats thirteen loaves without Grace and Rav Nahman rebukes him; one real act and a verbal response, mainly halakhic speech.
A one-line report that Rabbi appointed two brothers over the charity fund, cited as evidence; a single act with no continuation.
Rav Mordekhai goes from sage to sage with his question and rebukes them all; there is movement and conflict, but it is mainly scholarly dialogue.
Rav Huna hears a man grinding a millstone on Chol HaMoed and curses him; one event and a verbal reaction, then a halakhic comment.
The incident of Rav Yehuda's seal and Shmuel's order to deface it is only alluded to as a legal difficulty; one event and an order whose outcome is implied.
Rava testing his students with a contradiction between mishnayot is teaching and legal discussion, with no event.
R. Yirmeya's far-fetched question leads to his removal from the study hall: a speech act followed by one real consequence, told in a single line.
Rav Pappi's permission and Rava's objection are a ruling and standard rabbinic critique, followed by a report of Rava's own practice; no narrated change.
Rava teaches, Rav Pappa challenges him, and Rava publicly retracts through an interpreter; mostly teaching speech, but with an act and a change.
R. Ile'a searches among R. Eliezer's students for corroboration and finally R. Eliezer b. Yaakov agrees; a first-person account of events, but about transmitting a teaching.
The hunters' practice and their coming before R. Yehuda b. Beteira for a ruling; coming before a rabbi and being ruled on is the only event.
Ravina's eyewitness account of Rav Ashi donning tefillin at night and their exchange; one act plus dialogue, cited as evidence of his view.
Rav Huna's instruction to the merchants is legal advice, followed by Gemara analysis; no event is narrated.
R. Yitzhak Nappaha teaches publicly and Rav Sheshet becomes angry that the teaching was not attributed; speech with an emotional reaction and conflict.
A narrative about Miriam's prophecy, Moses's birth and her father's reactions: an exegetical retelling of a biblical episode.
Elijah's conversation with Rav Yehuda about the sins in Nehardea is almost all dialogue, with events only mentioned, then drifts into exegesis.
A bare report of what Rav did (threw date pits to animals), cited as evidence for a halakhic inference; nothing follows.
Exegetical narrative about the biblical Palti and Michal (sword in the bed); segment 3 is Gemara exegesis of verses.
A generic, habitual exchange of insults in Rabbi Yehuda's locale cited as evidence of local stringency; no event or change.
Rabbi asks Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon a halakhic question on the road and they answer; a setting plus question and answer is not a story.
Shmuel demands a source from Rav Mattana and receives a derivation; ordinary scholarly question and answer.
A single report of a seller calling out his wares, cited to identify a plant; no development.

Mostly a description of recurring Temple signs during and after Shimon HaTzaddik's tenure, with one incident (a priest who grabbed his fellow's portion and was nicknamed 'son of hamtzan' until his death) giving minimal event and consequence; segment 6 is verse commentary.
Rava sees Abaye bow and corrects him, then a report of their practice; ordinary halakhic correction with no further event or change.
Rabbi Yehuda raises an objection to Rabbi Akiva who retracts his teaching; speech and quasi-speech only, without conflict beyond scholarly discourse.
A report of what Rabbi Yishmael's father said/did, cited as halakhic evidence; nothing follows.
One act (Rabbi Ami seizing a sack of dinars) followed by the Gemara's legal discussion of it; no continuation or change.
A host's question passed to Rava and his ruling; a case brought before a rabbi with nothing else narrated.
Habitual practices of Rava and Mar son of Ravina and Rav Ashi's report about blessings; customs that lead nowhere.
A document comes before Rabbi, he comments, and Zunin explains the custom; a case before a rabbi with only speech following.
Lost meat, a question before Rav Nahman and his ruling; coming before the rabbi is the only event besides the ruling.
A single reported act of Rav Pappa cited as a halakhic challenge, then the Gemara's resolution.
Rabbi Yehuda Nesia sends a question to Rabbi Tarfon and receives a ruling; a halakhic query and answer.
Rabbi Yohanan denies a statement and Rabba bar bar Hana insists he said it; a scholarly dispute in speech only.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's habitual practice of reciting protective verses, followed by legal discussion; a custom that leads nowhere.
An incident merely alluded to as a case before Rabbi, who combined the testimonies; a case and ruling with no other narrated action.
Abaye's boast is followed by a sage's halakhic question and his answer; ordinary scholarly question and answer with no event beyond speech.
A setting (R. Elazar's arrival) framing a question and answer about who taught Rav; no conflict and no event beyond the exchange.
A report that the tanna'im were asked and taught two versions; no narrated incident.
Shmuel HaKatan decrees a fast, rain falls after sunset, the people misread it and he corrects them: events with a change and a response.
A report of two elders' practices and their reasons; nothing happens and nothing follows.
Ulla's lodging only frames Rava's challenge and Ulla's answer; standard scholarly question and answer.
Mainly a legal debate between students, but Rav Idi bar Avin wakes from dozing and intervenes, calling them children; a small real event within speech.
An exegetical narrative of David and Hushai built on the biblical text; biblical characters, not post-biblical sages.
Sages rebuke Rabbi Akiva's exegesis; ordinary scholarly back-and-forth without events.
Within a list of testimonies, an incident (a rooster stoned in Jerusalem for killing a person) is only alluded to as evidence.
A bare eyewitness report of Rabbi hanging his phylacteries, cited as evidence and then discussed.
Rav Hiyya bar Ashi's habitual practice cited as halakhic evidence; nothing follows.
An elder's statement about how R. Yohanan introduced a topic; teaching only.
A dialogue between Rabbi and R. Natan with conflict, followed by Rabbi's admission of youthful insolence and retraction; mainly speech with implied change.
A question asked in a cemetery and the halakhic answer; setting plus question and answer.
A planter's claim brought before a rabbi and the ensuing ruling and debate; coming before the rabbi is the only event, with no further narrated change.
Rava, confronted with Ravin's letter, appoints an amora and publicly retracts his teaching; mainly speech but with an action and change.
Alexa dies in Lod, all Israel gathers to eulogize him, and R. Tarfon prevents them: several events with a response, though cited as a legal difficulty.
A question put to R. Yohanan in Sidon and his answer; question and answer only.
Rabbi reports a word usage he heard while travelling, cited for exegesis; no incident.
An exchange between the emperor and R. Yehoshua ben Hananya with a challenge and a refusal; mainly speech with some conflict, no narrated event beyond speaking.
Legal-historical discussion identifying ben Zakkai; the examination incident is only cited, and the passage is the Gemara's analysis of it.
A bird fell into kamka and Rav Hinnana permitted it; one event and a ruling, followed by Rava's praise and legal reasoning, with no further change.
Shmuel finds Rav Yehuda weeping and they talk; an emotional state is an event, but the passage is mainly dialogue and exegesis.
Bare reports of two rulings permitting sleeping outside the sukka; no narrated action or change beyond the ruling.
A report that Rabban Gamliel's court voted to nullify, followed by ordinary scholarly question and answer.
Rabbis rule per Zekharya and are rebuked, one threatened with punishment; mainly speech, but with real conflict and a ruling actually issued.
A narrated incident: thieves come, the bailee hands over the captives' purse, the case comes to Rabba who exempts him; the cow-case shape of an incident with actions followed by a ruling.
Rav Nahman falls silent, Rava leaves, and he then realizes his answer; minimal events and change, mainly speech.
Rav Huna's wife comes to trial before Rav Nahman, who faces a dilemma and contrives to have a duck thrown at him so he can rise; actions with purpose and resolution.
A sale with a guarantee, a negotiation, then creditors seize the field and a flood destroys the best land; an actual incident with several events and change.
Two incidents cited briefly as evidence about scroll binding (Baitos ben Zunin; a scroll deemed fit); bare reports with no development.
A report of Shmuel's repeated practice of reciting kiddush again, cited as evidence of his view.
Rav Nahman visits Sura, is asked and rules, and the exchange is reported to Rav Huna with some friction; mainly speech with a visit as the event.
A report that the Sages voted in the upper story in Lod, giving a halakhic conclusion; no narrative development.
Rav Avya's hand is dislocated while sitting before Rav Yosef, he asks about positions, and meanwhile the hand heals; events and a change, followed by their exchange about it.
A brick falls into the oven and R. Hiyya speaks an indirect instruction; one event and a statement whose outcome is only implied, plus Rava's dictum.
Mareimar collects a ketubah from orphans' property and the rest is standard scholarly challenge and answer.
Reports of what R. Yohanan and R. Yannai did, cited as practice with colleagues' disagreement, then Gemara discussion; nothing follows.
Women come before Rabbi and Rav with a complaint and receive a ruling; coming before the rabbi is the only event.
An eyewitness report of what R. Yohanan did (bit and threw his nails), cited as evidence for halakha; no one responds and nothing follows.
The Sages asked the tannaim and they answered: a quasi-speech-act question and answer with no event or conflict.
Rav appointing a disseminator to teach his opposing view is teaching, i.e. speech; no narrated event or change.
Habitual practices of Rav Huna and Rav Ashi with their rationale; customs that lead to no one-time event or change.
A fragment of the larger innkeeper story: the sages come to a house named Bala and do not enter; one real event plus exegetical reasoning, part of a story rather than all of it.
Rabba permits a tereifa and buys its meat, his wife challenges him and he defends himself; real acts and a conflict, but mainly dialogue with no change.
A certain man promised his land to one person, then went and sold it to another, and Rav Yosef ruled: the incident-plus-ruling shape of Jeff's cow case, with two narrated actions.
Rav Eina's public teaching is denounced by Rabba, who orders his interpreter removed; speech with sharper-than-ordinary conflict, so borderline.
Rabban Gamliel the Elder dies and Onkelos burns a fortune in his honor; a real incident cited as precedent, with a response but little development, between bare report and story.
A heretic's taunt and R. Abbahu's cutting retort: speech only, but with genuine conflict.
A habitual custom (the emperor's ladies singing whenever R. Abbahu came) that leads to no event or change.
An incident only named, then an ordinary scholarly exchange between Rav Yosef and Abaye about an objection; no narrated action or change.
A tanna recites a baraita before Rav and a question is raised; teaching and legal discussion, no event.
Rav eats dates and throws the pits into the oven and R. Hiyya rebukes him; one real event then speech, with the outcome left as a legal question.
A halakhic dispute, a question put to R. Bisa and his answer, then a verse applied in praise; quasi-speech-acts with no conflict beyond ordinary debate.
Levi in the bathhouse sees a man bang his head and remarks on it; one real event followed by speech, cited as evidence for a legal point.
Rabbi's recollection that they ate fruit outside the sukka is a report of practice cited as evidence in the legal discussion; nothing follows.
Exegetical narrative about biblical figures (Zedekiah son of Chenaanah, Naboth's spirit, Ahab and Jehoshaphat), outside the rabbinic/post-biblical scope.
A judge rules, a scholar challenges him and threatens to bring a letter, then goes before Rav Hama, who upholds the ruling; mainly speech with conflict and some action but no change.
A dream reported and interpreted: a question and answer in speech with no conflict and no narrated event.
A halakhic question-and-answer between Ravina and Rav Ashi about preparing knives; Rav Ashi's own practice is only cited, with no event or conflict.
R. Elazar's dream of R. Yohanan is cited only to validate an exegesis; a bare report with nothing following.
A visit that frames a question about the order of blessings and Rava's textual answer; setting plus question and answer is not a story (Shabbat 147a ruling).
A man's vow is brought before Rav Hisda who rules; coming before the rabbi and the ruling are the only events, cited to infer his view.

A firstborn sells the property, the purchasers beat the orphans who ate dates, the relatives protest and Rava rules: several actions, conflict and resolution. Segment 3 is the Gemara's analysis (R-B4).
Ravina asks Rav Ashi about land with synagogue ruins and receives a ruling; no other narrated action or change.
Scholarly exchange between Rav Hisda and Avimei about a mishna's difficulty; ordinary dialogue, no event.
R. Yehoshua b. Levi reports three teachings the Angel of Death told him; a cited dictum with no narrated action or consequence.
A Levite's habitual snatching is reported to Rav, who only remarks on it; nothing follows, and the passage serves the legal discussion.
A heretic mocks God to R. Abbahu and a student asks a question, setting up his answer; speech with conflict and no further event.
A blind neighbor habitually judged and R. Yohanan said nothing; a custom that leads nowhere, cited as a legal difficulty.
A land dispute: claim, witnesses for two years, Rav Nahman's ruling; a case before a rabbi with no narrated action beyond the litigation.
An animal is brought before Rav who rules, then Rav Kahana and Rav Asi meet the owner and comment; mostly a ruling with a small follow-up encounter.
Rabbi asks R. Shimon b. Halafta why he did not visit and he answers with a poetic description of old age; speech without conflict or event.
Students ask R. Perida about his longevity and he lists his habitual practices, followed by Gemara commentary; no event.
A needle found in a lung is brought before the rabbis, who decline to rule; a case brought to rabbis with legal reasoning, no further event.
A six-year-old prodigy answers a series of halakhic questions; question and answer without conflict or event.
Rav Hisda's statement about his own handwashing practice and reward, cited as evidence; a bare report of practice.
Rav has his crop harvested on the festival and Shmuel hears and is dismayed: two events and an emotional reaction, but little development before the Gemara's analysis.
Agrippa's steward asks R. Eliezer two halakhic questions and receives answers; question and answer with no narrated event.
Levi reads from an improper Megilla before Rav Yehuda, who states the ruling; one event then a ruling with nothing changing afterwards.
Rav Ashi's duck enters the reeds and emerges bloodied (an event with a change), then only a ruling follows; events but little development.
An animal is brought to Ravina and he rules; coming before the rabbi is the only event.
Rabbi Sheila lectures, and after he leaves Rav sets up an interpreter and publicly teaches the opposite; implicit conflict but mainly teaching (speech).
A custom of city dwellers bequeathing lulavim is cited as evidence in a halakhic dispute; a practice that leads nowhere.
A bare mention that a jug once burst, cited as evidence in legal discussion.
A man comes before Rava with a question and Rava rules; no further narrated action or change.
Rava's directive to the residents of Mehoza is a ruling with its rationale, not a narrated event.
Rabba's one-line eyewitness report of seeing the angel Ridya; a wonder-sighting that is an open edge between report and story.
Part of the account of the students' visit reporting R. Elazar ben Azarya's lecture, ending in R. Yehoshua's reaction; almost entirely teaching (speech).
An elder relays a tradition to Rabbi Zeira within the legal argument; ordinary scholarly exchange.
Baraita incident: the Temple candelabrum was overweight and refined eighty times until it reached a talent; events with a change, but cited as evidence with little drama.
Abaye changes his practice of where he prays after hearing a teaching; a change in practice, but mainly a report of his habit and speech.
The deception of the reed in Rava's court is only alluded to and must be filled in from commentary.
Rava proposes a historical circumstance (the persecution directive) as an explanation within legal give-and-take, not a narrated event.
