R. Zeira's repeated questions, R. Asi's silence, then R. Asi teaching and admitting the halakha came back to him; mainly speech with some change.
The Baitos ben Zunen sale under R. Elazar ben Azarya's direction is cited as precedent and disputed; real events but sketchy and with little change.
Rabba's instruction to those binding the Exilarch's lulav is a ruling, not an event.
A seller sees the buyer's distress and reassures him; a small incident with an emotional reaction and response, followed by legal discussion that is not part of the story.
Abaye's report that he saw certain bills of sale, cited as evidence of Rabba's view.
A corpse is permitted to be moved (a ruling), then a challenge and a sharp retort; one event and a ruling with ordinary halakhic dispute, nothing further narrated.
A household custom of reassembling a bed, then a sage's question and Rava's answer; a custom leading nowhere plus Q&A.
Reish Lakish shows a coin, which only frames a legal exchange about indirect liability; standard rabbinic dialogue without conflict or change.
Rav Huna's sale of a cow is reported as practice, followed by a question and his justification and a halakhic proof; no change follows.
A case of a document's witnesses brought for ratification, then Ravina and Rav Ashi's legal discussion; no further narrated action.
The emperor's question and R. Yehoshua's enigmatic answer about old age are speech alone with no real conflict or event.
Two cases of a borrowed axe that broke, each brought before a rabbi and ruled on, then a challenge; one event plus ruling, nothing changes after.
Rav Sheshet's instruction to his servant is cited as evidence of his view; speech and practice, no event.
A prayer leader acts against the majority view, Rabba rebukes him and he defends himself; one real act followed by a confrontational exchange, mainly speech.
R. Yehuda's report that he read as a minor is cited as proof and rejected; a bare report used as evidence with no continuation.
R. Yosei b. R. Hanina's instruction to his servant to store produce illustrates a halakha; speech/practice only.
Rava praises R. Aha, R. Nahman has him brought, R. Aha comes and stumps him with questions until Nahman says 'leave me alone'; some events and a change, but mainly dialogue.
Shmuel meeting Rav's students only frames a question and answer about halakha; a setting plus Q&A is not a story.
R. Ila, climbing stairs, overhears a child reciting a verse and reacts with dread; one real event and a reaction, followed by exegesis, with little development.
Rav Shmuel bar Bisna's refusing wine and beer is a report of his practice cited for its halakhic rationale; nothing follows.
R. Yehuda Nesia decrees a fast, prays without result, laments, is distressed, and rain comes; multiple events with a causal change.
A report that three sages measured the Jordan stones is cited as evidence for a calculation; a bare report with no continuation.
R. Hiyya throws a clod at the moon and addresses it, and Rabbi sends him to sanctify the month; real actions but little causality or change.
Rabbi's question to R. Yehoshua b. Korha and his answer about longevity are teaching dialogue; the brief retort is ordinary discourse, no event.
Rav recounts Rabbi changing his ruling overnight, Rav retracting and Levi, absent, not; mainly speech-acts with some change, cited as evidence for a dictum.
A real case: the ewe drags its legs, two sages disagree, it is inspected and found cut. Events with a finding, but the passage is mainly a legal dispute that ends in a halakhic ruling.
A man's habitual saying leads to an inspection that reveals his lineage. There is an event and an outcome, but causality and change are minimal.
An actual dispute in which the creditor goes ahead and consumes the produce, followed by two amoraim's opinions. There is an incident beyond the ruling, but the passage is mostly legal discussion.
Hillel sees a skull floating and speaks to it. One real event followed by speech, with little development; R. Yohanan's dictum is not part of it.
An actual event, an old man crushed in Hillel's day, and the Passover being named for it. Sketched very briefly, with little development.
Rav Nahman decrees a fast, no rain comes, he despairs, and then the rain comes. Several events and a clear change.
A polemical exchange between a magus and Ameimar. It is speech only, but there is conflict.
An encounter that frames ordinary scholarly back-and-forth about combining testimonies. The jibe is normal Talmudic discourse, so nothing happens beyond speech.
An exegetical narrative about Moses, Zipporah and the angels Af and Heima, built on biblical events.
Rav Se'oram's habitual seizing of improper people, approved by Rava with a proof text. Real acts, but customary and leading only to a ruling.
Someone vows to go up, does so, and learns the ruling was reported in reverse. Mainly about transmitting teachings, with a journey as the event.
A historical account of successive educational ordinances, ending with Yehoshua ben Gamla's reform. There is change over time, but it is an institutional report rather than a narrated incident.
One sage tells another of a neighbourly custom about leaning trees. Speech only, with no conflict and no event.
A poor man comes and Rav Pappa does not attend to him; Rav Sama protests and the rest is legal discussion of the baraita. One event, some conflict, then discussion.
Rabbi Zeira arrives and has a scholarly exchange with Rav Asi about whether Reish Lakish disagreed. A setting plus question and answer, with no conflict.
A brief report of Rav eating breaded dove, cited inside the legal give-and-take as evidence. No development.
Two incidents brought before Rava. In the second, wine is bought and ferments before the ruling, more than a bare case. Each still ends in a ruling and discussion.
A sharecropper makes a stipulation and then leaves a third of the field fallow, followed by competing legal opinions. The incident has actions, but it is mainly a legal case.
Rav Pappa tries the remedies without success, an Arab gives him another, he follows it and is healed. A first-person narrative with several actions and a change.
The courtyard's collective cries against or for named priests. Mainly speech with conflict, plus brief reports of conduct.
A teaching exchange between Rabbi Shimon bar Yohai and his students about why the generation deserved annihilation; question and answer only, no event.
A narrated incident with several actions and a change (buyer takes the donkey, fails to sell it, it is injured on return), then Rav Nahman's ruling; the cow-case shape.
One real event (Rav Ashi sells his forest to a fire temple) followed by Ravina's challenge and an answer; mainly speech after a single act.
A habit (avoiding the wall) followed by a one-time occasion when Rav Adda bar Ahava visits, but what follows is dialogue with the outcome only implied.
The 'incident of the orchard' is cited as a legal precedent with a mortgage, years of use and a threat, but no outcome is narrated; a partially told incident used as evidence.
A woman distressed by her son takes an impulsive oath, unworthy men press to marry her, and the Sages rule; several actions and a change before the ruling.
A single reported event (Nehunya's son died of thirst) appended to the preceding story and used for exegesis; an alluded fragment rather than a full story.
A sick-visit setting framing a halakhic question and answer about Rabbi Yosei's view; per Shabbat 147a a setting plus question and answer is not a story.
An exposed jug is brought to Rav Hilkiya bar Tovi and he rules; coming before the rabbi and the ruling are the only events.
A planter's stipulation and loss serve as a case for a legal dispute among Amoraim; one event then rulings, with nothing further narrated.
A girl found among barrels holding froth, and Rava's ruling; a single finding followed by a ruling, no further action or change.
A woman finds blood and comes before Rabbi Yannai who instructs her; a case brought to a rabbi and his ruling.
Embedded incident: a tied document before Rabbi, his son's suggestion, and Rabbi opening it to find the date; a real event with some change, but cited within a legal argument and mostly speech.
Habitual practice of Rav and Rav Nahman when visiting towns, reported as custom with no one-time event following.
A scholarly debate between Rabbi Yirmeya and Rabbi Zeira over accepting Rami bar Hama's explanation; ordinary rabbinic dialogue without events.
Two purchases at a pagan fair and a mutual rebuke from a misunderstanding, then a legal explanation; real acts and conflict but mainly speech and no change narrated.
Students' questions to Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai and his explanations of Torah laws, with Rav Yosef's objection; teaching, not events.
A needle found in a liver and the rabbis' halakhic discussion of its status; a case and its ruling only.
A hypothetical baraita case ('one who says...') with a tannaitic dispute; not an event.
A ruling reported before King Shapur, who praises Rabbi Shimon; speech only, no event or conflict.
The Neharde'a goats incident (goats ate barley, owner seized them, Shmuel's father ruled) is alluded to as a precedent inside a legal objection; events exist but it is only sketched.
Elijah's advice to Rav Yehuda is pure speech with no conflict or event, followed by halakhic exposition.
Rabbi Yohanan fell ill, prepared the remedy on Shabbat and was cured, then was challenged; real events with change but embedded in legal discussion.
Mostly an exchange of halakhic queries and replies in several versions, but it ends with an event and change: because of his answer Rabbi Yirmeya was readmitted to the study hall.
The Sages gathered the items Rabbi Eliezer declared pure, burned them before him, and ostracized him: multiple actions, conflict and change.
Rabbi Hananya Kara's report of his practice and the permission he received is cited as evidence; no narrated incident with change.
Mainly a dialogue between Rava and his students, but events are mentioned (they mastered tractates, bought land) and Rava responds.
Akiva's safe ascent and the angels seeking to push him away until God intervened is a fragment of the Pardes story; the following segments are exegetical commentary on it.
An exegetical narrative about Solomon's marriage and Gabriel planting a reed, built on biblical events, not about rabbis or post-biblical figures.
One act (Rav Yosef moving beams by day) followed by an ordinary halakhic challenge and answer; nothing changes.
A habitual practice of a priest in Rabbi Yohanan's neighborhood cited as a legal objection; no incident.
A setting (Abaye found Rav Yosef sleeping under a canopy) followed by standard halakhic challenge and answer; no change.
Brief incidents where a visiting rabbi moved a lamp and the host became angry (an emotional reaction), plus Rabbi Abbahu's deference; events with minimal development.
A man's remark leads to a suit before Rav Nahman and his ruling; a case brought to a rabbi and ruled on, with no further change.
A case brought before Rabba, his ruling, a scholarly challenge and his silence, then Gemara commentary; ordinary legal give-and-take.
A mocking exchange between two heretics, Sason and Simha; speech only but with conflict.
A man came before Rabbi Ami, was sent to Rabbi Abba bar Memel and received a ruling; coming before a rabbi is the only event.
King Shapur mocks Shmuel and Shmuel retorts; speech only, but with conflict.
Rav Beruna once juxtaposed redemption and prayer and laughed all day: an act with an emotional reaction, cited as evidence inside Rabbi El'a's instruction to Ulla.
A man reports an official's threat to Rava and receives a ruling; the case before the rabbi and his ruling are the only events, and nothing follows.
Rabbi Hiyya's habitual practice of telling people to fatten or thin a youth; a custom cited for the law, no one-time event or change.
A dispute brought with witnesses is a legal case framing a ruling; coming to court is the only event and nothing else changes.
One act (taking the share) brought before Abaye, followed by his ruling and rebuke; one event then a ruling, with no further change.
Rabbi Ami breaking a bowl is a single act cited as evidence for a legal view inside the give-and-take; nothing follows.
The goats damaging Rav Yosef's property is a real event, but the rest is an exchange of speech with Abaye and nothing changes.
Rava testing his students with a contradiction is teaching and scholarly discussion, speech without an event.
A one-line report of a giant snake in Shapur's day, cited as a refutation in the legal discussion, with no narrative development.
A question put to Rabbi Tanhum framing a homily; a setting plus question and exegesis, not a story.
Rabbi Zeira arrives, challenges Rabbi Ami, who is astonished and then answers; mainly dialogue, but with an arrival and an emotional reaction.
Rabbis' established practice in their towns is reported and the Sages rule on it; a practice followed by a ruling, nothing further happens.
Rav Asi's practice of reciting havdala is cited as evidence of his view in a legal discussion.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's rebuke of Rabbi Akiva over an exegesis is ordinary scholarly dispute, followed by Gemara analysis.
Rav Sheshet's single instruction to be run past an ashera is cited as a precedent and analyzed; nothing follows.
Rabba's habitual practice of opening with a joke before teaching; a custom leading to no change.
A maidservant's remark cited only as lexical evidence for a word's meaning; a speech act with no event.
A passerby's aphorism and Shmuel's matching verse; pure speech with no event or conflict.
Rabbi Mani's stringent purchasing practice and an elder's approving remark; a reported practice with no change or conflict.
Rabbi Abba's instruction to his servant is cited to infer his legal position; speech only, followed by analysis.
Rabbi Zeira saw the Sages running, judged them, heard a teaching and changed his own behavior; a first-person account with real change but mostly thought and speech.
Rabbi Abbahu's ear pain is one event followed by an instruction that turns into a medical recipe; no outcome is narrated.
A question sent to the Land of Israel and its answer, then Rav Yosef refuses the post, Rabba reigns 22 years, Rav Yosef succeeds him and shows deference throughout. Several actions and a change.
Rav Yehuda sees feces and tells Ravina to examine it. That is a setting plus an instruction, a ruling with no further action or change.
Rava's order to his attendant is cited as evidence of his view inside legal give-and-take. It is a bare report that leads nowhere.
A tanna recites a baraita and Rav Adda bar Ahava corrects its wording. This is ordinary scholarly dialogue with no event and no conflict.
The incident of Rabbi Nehorai going to Usha to testify is only alluded to as evidence in the legal discussion. It is a single act with its details left to reconstruction.
R. Yishmael b. R. Yosei falls ill and Rabbi sends a request, which he answers with his father's teachings. There is a real event, but the passage is mainly an exchange of teachings.
Rava falls ill and gives his family instructions that change as his illness worsens. There are events, but they are mostly speech and little changes.
A man comes before Rabba bar Rav Huna, is asked a question and has his vow dissolved. The only event is coming before the rabbi, then a ruling.
Abaye finds Rabba sliding his son along a donkey's back and challenges him, and Rabba defends the act legally. There is one real act, followed by halakhic discussion.
A king parable that illustrates Hannah's prayer. It is part of an exegetical narrative on a biblical episode, not a story about sages.
Rav Hisda recalls being disparaged by Avimi over a halakha, then the explanation follows. This is standard rabbinic back-and-forth with no narrated event.
Ravina permits beer, Rav Hiyya pours wine instead, and Ravina is unconcerned. There are events, but weak change, embedded in a legal discussion.
A question is sent to Rav Huna, he dies before answering, and his son answers in his name. Rav Huna's death is a real event, but the passage is mainly a transmitted ruling.
A sharecropper plants wheat instead of sesame and gets a comparable yield, then the rabbis discuss the ruling. The incident has more than one action, but what follows is legal discussion.
A letter relays Ukvan's complaint that his brother wronged him and summons the brother to Tiberias. It is mainly speech, with conflict and an alluded wrong.
An elder's habitual practice of smoothing salt with pig fat is cited as evidence. It is a custom that leads nowhere.
Bar Hedya's eyewitness report of linen being laundered at Tiberias is cited as evidence of practice. No one responds and nothing follows.
Rav Kahana hides under Rav's bed, overhears him, speaks out, and Rav sends him away. There are several actions, conflict and a consequence.
The angels question God and God answers. This is an aggadic dialogue explaining a practice, with no narrated event.
Ravin repeats a halakha and R. Yirmeya rebukes the Babylonians before citing a teaching. A sharp retort is ordinary Talmudic discourse, and the journey only sets the scene.
The tail of the Rabbi Zakkai story: the inheritances of wine as reward. Real events with a change, but it is only the outcome of a story begun in the context.
Ravina's twelve-month delay is cited as a precedent. It is a single act with no response or change.
The Rav Pappa incident is only named, and the translator fills it in. That makes it an alluded incident.
A legal answer that explains Rav Huna's ruling. No narrated event.
Rav Kahana reads before Rav, Rav sighs, and Kahana draws an inference. Real events but little change; the rest is exegesis.
Rabba decrees a fast and no rain comes. The rest is mainly his speech in a tense exchange with the people.
An exclamation and a halakhic objection. Only speech.
A man mortgages an orchard, the orchard ages, then Abaye and Rava dispute. Events then legal discussion, with no resolution narrated.
Rav Ashi's brief first-person report of a dream and his rise to greatness. An event and a change, minimally told.
Rabba sells a donkey and Abaye questions it. One act followed by ordinary halakhic back-and-forth.
A proverbial announcement and a recalled saying. No incident.
Rava bar Livai's injury and Rava's explanation of it are cited as evidence of Rava's view. Events with weak causality.
Rabbi Zeira relays Rabbi Hiyya's ruling and Rabbi retracts. Mainly speech, with a change of view; segments 3-4 are legal discussion.
A dispute over which book to study, Levi is compelled, Psalms is brought, and Levi takes Rabbi's teaching as permission to leave. Several actions with conflict and change.
Two brothers divide an estate, one builds a wall, there is a complaint, and Rav Hama rules. Real events but nothing changes after the ruling.
Legal discussion that mentions in passing that Rav Nahman ruled in a case. No narrated incident.
An exegetical narrative about the biblical Jonathan, Micah's priest, and King David. Segment 4 is the Gemara's commentary.
Basket sellers are blocked by the townspeople and come before Ravina, who rules. Events then a ruling and halakhic qualification.
A woman confesses to Rav Hisda, he predicts her death, and she does not die (or, in the other version, dies). Events with an outcome; segment 3 is commentary.
A stain case in which Rabbi Meir and Rabbi attribute the stain to a source. A case and a ruling with no other narrated action.
An orphan lease whose wine soured, then only a legal comparison between Rav Kahana and Rav Ashi; one incident followed by discussion, nothing changes.
Rabbi and R. Hiyya walk, veer aside, see R. Yehuda ben Kenosa striding ahead, reach him and Rabbi confronts him: several actions, conflict and a resolution.
A setting (Rav Aha enters a meal) framing a halakhic exchange about who blesses; like Shabbat 147a, the setting plus question and answer is not a story.
Rav Huna sees a man drink water before havdala and rebukes him: one real event, then mainly speech, cited as a halakhic position.
People come before Rav Yitzhak bar Ami and he rules on path width; coming before a rabbi and the ruling are the only events.
Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef buys a utensil and is told immersion is not required; one event then a ruling, no stated outcome.
A dialogue between a heretic and R. Hanina about Balaam's age, with no event and no real conflict; speech only.
A man testifies before R. Hanina that someone is a firstborn; a case brought to a rabbi with question and answer, nothing narrated changes.
A man resolves to go up to Eretz Yisrael to hear a ruling from its source, travels, and learns it was misreported: a real journey, but mostly a halakhic Q&A.
Four sages need a head, set a contest, all but Abaye are refuted, Rabba sees it and calls on Abaye to begin: actions and a change in status.
A halakhic debate between R. Yohanan and Reish Lakish ending in silence and a quip; ordinary scholarly back-and-forth, not conflict in the R-C2 sense.
R. Elazar b. R. Yosei's one-line testimony that he saw the curtain in Rome, cited as evidence for a halakha; nothing follows.
A one-line eyewitness wonder by Rabba bar bar Hana (the I-myself-saw shape left open under R-C5); an observation with little event or change.
Reports of how Rabba, R. Yohanan and R. Asi habitually trimmed kidney fat, then legal discussion; practice cited as evidence.
A halakhic question and answer between Rav Aha and Rav Ashi; no event.
Legal objection citing a ruling of Rava and a sent ruling of Rav Huna bar Avin; precedents alluded to as evidence, no narrative.
R. Yohanan's saying about his tenth son's bone is cited only to attribute an interpretation; no event is narrated.
Levi checking his collection of baraitot and the ensuing legal argument; a source citation, not a story.
R. Yannai sees a man give charity publicly and rebukes him for shaming the poor man: one real event, then speech with conflict, cited as an exemplum.
An incident of someone swallowing a leech and R. Nehemya permitting heating water on Shabbat: one event followed by a ruling, nothing further narrated.
A man's habitual saying and the Sages' inference about his lineage; no event, nothing follows.
A teaching reported before R. Yohanan, his silence and Abbahu's inference; speech only, no conflict or narrated change.
A brief incident cited as evidence: a man crossed water and his shoes shrank and feet shriveled. Real events but barely narrated.
Setting (Rav Ashi finds Rav Kahana building) framing a question and answer about Rava's view; ordinary halakhic exchange.
An animal brought before Rav Ashi and a ruling discussed; coming before a rabbi is the only event.
Mainly legal speech, but framed by events: R. Yirmeya dozing, the students talking, and him waking to correct them.
A baraita taught and R. Yohanan's dismissive retort; ordinary scholarly exchange, no event.
R. Yona's habitual secret prayer leads to rain and a concealing exchange with his household; a habit that causes change.
Post-biblical narrative of Nicanor's threats, Hasmonean victory and the hanging of his thumbs and toes; actions and change.
An incident only alluded to: a man completed 365 naziriteships and died, cited as evidence in a legal discussion.
A visit framing an exchange of vow formulas, then Gemara analysis; speech without conflict or narrated change.
A full story (Esau blocks Jacob's burial, Hushim kills him) but an exegetical narrative about biblical characters.
Mainly halakhic dialogue, but with a setting and a pointed personal insult by Reish Lakish against R. Elazar, giving some conflict.
Rav Nahman's jug and a case asked of Rav Asi serve a legal discussion; a question and ruling with no narrated change.
The Sages wished to rule and R. Yannai objected; a legal debate, no event.
Mainly speech, but Rav Yosef angrily turns his face away; an emotional reaction with conflict in a halakhic exchange.
Accompanying a teacher only sets up a question; setting plus question is not a story.
Rav's instruction on Kahana's visit is cited as evidence in the legal give-and-take; a bare report with nothing following.
Rav Kahana's remark alludes to his marriage leading to his forced exile; the incident is only alluded to, told through speech.
Rav Nahman disparages Saul, is shown nightmares, apologizes, and again until it stops; actions, causality and change.
Reports of rabbis' practices with breaking bread, plus a routine question and answer; nothing follows from the acts.
Description of a donated chandelier and a recurring effect; no narrated event.
A one-line report that his father's goats sneezed from the incense, cited as evidence; no development or change.
The marten-and-pit story is only alluded to; its content is supplied by the translator/commentaries.
A Temple custom recurring every seventy years and legal discussion, plus Rava's drinking practice; no one-time event.
Rav Aha bar Yaakov's habitual practice and saying, with the Gemara's comment; nothing follows.
Rav Yosef turns his face away in anger (conflict in a halakhic exchange), and Rav Amram's fringes incident is alluded to as precedent.
Ordinary scholarly exchange: a group ruling, a challenge, praise and a counter-remark; no event beyond speech.
A setting (Sages entering the vineyard in Yavne) framing a teaching; speech without conflict or event.
Mainly a polemical dialogue between the emperor and Rabban Gamliel with conflict; the emperor's groaning is the only event.
An incident (Rav bar Shaba visiting Ravina, who did not interrupt hallel) cited briefly as evidence; minimal events and no change.
Ravya bar Kisi died on the day of the dispute and the scholars made a mnemonic of it; a real event with weak development.
A visit framing a question and answer about blessing practice; setting plus Q&A is not a story.
Powerful men seized sycamore trunks by force and the owners responded by consecrating them; events and a response, but described generally rather than as one incident.
An incident (upper victims dead, lower alive) is only alluded to as precedent within a legal ruling.
A one-line report that the High Priest's voice was heard in Jericho, followed by a distance note; no development.
Heretics challenge Rabban Gamliel and reject his proofs: dialogue with conflict, no event beyond speech.
An eyewitness report of seeing the frontplate in Rome, cited as evidence in a legal argument; nothing happens.
Rav Hisda recounts reciting Grace at the Exilarch's house and Rav Sheshet's angry reaction, which leads him to decline to teach; events, conflict and change.
An exegetical dialogue between Abraham and God built on Genesis 15; biblical figures, not rabbis.
A baraita alludes to an incident (the daughters preceded the sons) cited as evidence; the competition is only sketched, not narrated in full.
A Sadducee taunts Rabbi Hanina and he answers; pure speech, but with real polemical conflict.
Rav decrees a fast, no rain; the prayer leader prays and rain comes; Rav asks his merit and he tells it. Multiple events and change.
Rav Tahlifa acted on Shmuel's view and Rav rebuked it as corruption; one real event followed by a reaction, embedded in legal proof.
Ravina finds Mar bar Rav Ashi discarding berries and eating buds and challenges him; one observed act, then halakhic debate.
Rav Pappa makes an obvious remark and is laughed at, then draws a lesson; speech only, but being mocked is conflict.
A habitual practice of Rav Ami and Rav Asi with their reasoning; a custom that leads nowhere.
A man's wine got mixed and he came before Rav Hisda, who ruled; one event then a ruling, nothing further narrated.
Someone came before Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi who stated a ruling; coming before a rabbi is the only event.
Rabbi Zerika recounts visiting a house where they were served cooked organs and ate, cited as legal evidence; events but little change.
Binyamin the shepherd recited an Aramaic blessing and Rav ruled he fulfilled his duty; one act followed by a ruling and discussion.
Rav bar Shaba's interpretation is laughed at and Rav Kahana rebukes the laughers; speech-only with mocking conflict.
Two eyewitness wonders (goats sneezing; an old man smelling incense at Shiloh); the one-time visit is an event but minimal development.
Rav Yehuda's habitual act of removing a shoe brought rain, cited in a homiletic comparison; habit with an effect but no narrated episode.
Mar Zutra judged, erred and came before Rav Yosef who ruled; events beyond coming before the rabbi, but it is a precedent cited in legal give-and-take.
A clarifying exchange about what Rav said; ordinary scholarly dialogue without conflict or event.
Rav Safra recounts visiting Rabbi Abba, being fed the dissolved chicken and saved from vomiting by old wine; small events cited to illustrate the mishna.
Habitual practices of Abaye's mother and Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak's attendant cited as evidence; customs that lead nowhere.
Gentiles came before Rabba bar Avuh and he instructed them; coming before the rabbi and his instruction are the only content, cited as proof.
Ravin reports a teaching and Rabbi Yirmeya derides Babylonians and cites a baraita; standard rabbinic rebuke within legal discussion.
Ark, Table and Candelabrum of fire descend and Moses copies them: an exegetical narrative about a biblical episode, not a sage story.
A report of Rabbi Yohanan's occasional practice of declaring a fast to excuse himself, cited as legal evidence; nothing follows.
Rav Kahana's reflection on what he learned is pure speech with no event or conflict.
Rabba dozes and Abaye questions him; one small event (dozing) followed by dialogue citing the mishna, mainly speech.
The Nasi's house failed to inform them of a fast; this setting only frames a halakhic question and answer, with no change.
A man hides witnesses to trap a debtor, an exchange follows, and Rav Kahana rules; there is a real act but the rest is speech and a ruling with no narrated change.
One act (dragging a bench) prompts a halakhic challenge and discussion; ordinary rabbinic questioning, no change.
A heretic's mocking question and Berurya's sharp retort: speech only, but with conflict.
A one-line report that Rava compelled Rav Natan to give 400 dinars, cited as precedent; a single act with nothing following.
A fox clawing a ewe brought before the Sages for a ruling, cited inside legal give-and-take; one event plus a ruling.
Students' misunderstanding corrected by Rabbi Yirmeya: scholarly speech, no event or conflict.
Vow-annulment cases where someone comes before a rabbi, answers a question, and the vow is dissolved; coming before the rabbi and the ruling are the only events.
A brief question and answer between Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba and Rav, cited to show his status; speech with no conflict.
Rabba bar Rav Huna's visit only frames his halakhic practice of spreading a cloth before kiddush, cited as precedent; nothing develops.
Rabbi Yishmael's family habitually grazed in forests and judged alone and were destroyed; a habit that leads to a change, but told as a summary with weak narration.
Rav Yosef turns his face in disdain at Rav Huna's ruling; a gesture of conflict but mainly halakhic speech.
Rabbi Hanina goes to the villages and teaches a resolution of contradicting verses; teaching with no conflict or change.
